303	
304	
305	                                     Discussion
306	                                     To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that has investigated the relationship
307	                                     between the importance of a game and concussion incidence. Surprisingly, the results suggest
308	                                     that, except for RBs, players are not more likely to suffer concussions in games with playoff
309	                                     implications than in games without. Instead, a major modulator of concussion risk is the
310	                                     number of plays per game [21].
311	
312	
313	                                     Previous research has shown that TEs, RBs, CBs, and WRs have the highest rates of concussion,
314	                                     and passing positions overall have higher concussion incidence than running plays. This is
315	                                     attributed to the nature of collisions that occur in passing positions [1,22]. RBs did have higher
316	                                     concussion incidence in IH games, but contrary to expectations, the same effect was absent for
317	                                     TEs, CBs, and WRs. Due to the low sample size, further research will be necessary to validate
318	                                     and explain this phenomenon. However, one explanation is that there may be differences in
319	                                     fatigue and risk exposure inherent in various positions. For example, even though teams tend
320	                                     to throw the ball more often than they run it, an individual RB gets more touches per game than
321	                                     an individual receiver, increasing fatigue for the RB [7]. Furthermore, RBs get hit almost every
322	                                     time they touch the ball, increasing their exposure to concussion risk, whereas an individual
323	                                     WR gets fewer targets per game and gets hit on a lower percentage of those plays due to the
324	                                     prevailing rates of incomplete passes.
325	
326	
327	                                     The hypothesis for higher concussion incidence in IH games is predicated on the idea that
328	                                     players make riskier plays and/or increase the force of their tackles to increase their team’s
329	                                     chances of winning. The lack of significant differences both overall and at individual positions
330	                                     may be due to the naturally high-velocity impacts experienced at those positions accompanied
331	                                     by the highest concussion incidence. A previous study on concussion biomechanics
332	                                     demonstrated that a different concussion risk modulator, improved helmet manufacturing, can
333	                                     decrease concussion incidence for 16.6 mph and 20.8 mph impacts; however, for high-velocity
334	                                     impacts of 25.1 mph, the same improved helmet technology had zero effect on concussion
335	                                     incidence [23]. Since the player positions most vulnerable to concussion are also experiencing
336	                                     the highest velocity impacts, it may be more difficult for players to modulate their risk exposure
337	
338	
339	
340	2019 Hannah et al. Cureus 11(11): e6252. DOI 10.7759/cureus.6252                                                                          7 of 10
341	                                    than previously expected.
342	
343	
344	                                   There were a few assumptions made in this study that, if untrue, may explain why the
345	                                   importance of the game does not appear to modulate concussion incidence. The first is that the
346	                                   effect of game importance on concussion incidence would be modulated solely through
347	                                   modifications that players make at the individual level. However, a previous study had
348	                                   concluded that a team’s style of play influenced concussion incidence [7]. Certain coaching
349	                                   styles may limit an individual player’s ability to modulate their exposure to concussion-
350	                                   inducing collisions. With a larger dataset, further stratification of games across the offensive
351	                                   and defensive styles of play of each team would likely be a valuable investigation. It was also
352	                                   assumed that the importance of the game to the team’s playoff hopes would be the single
353	                                   element of influence on how inclined a player would be to risk injury to improve their team’s
354	                                   chances of winning. However, players who are in the last year of their contract may be
355	                                   motivated to demonstrate their full potential irrespective of team standings. Moreover, when
356	                                   games become unimportant from a playoff standpoint, coaches may give second and third-
357	                                   string players opportunities to showcase their abilities to management to increase their stock
358	                                   for the following year. These players are much more likely to risk injury to prove their
359	                                   worth. Finally, all players were assumed to have an equal ability to adjust their games to reduce
360	                                   their risk of injury. It has been previously shown that players with lesser skills suffer
361	                                   concussions more frequently than more skilled players [24,25]. If players with lesser skills are
362	                                   less able to mitigate concussion risk but receive more playing time in non-IH games, this would
363	                                   dampen any effect of the skilled players avoiding concussions in non-IH games.
364	
365	
366	                                   Limitations
367	                                   In addition to the limitations inherent in these assumptions, this study is also limited by low
368	                                   sample size in many of the game-type categories of interest, leading to unequal variances
369	                                   between groups. A study that involves more seasons with reliable concussion data would
370	                                   improve the accuracy and power of these analyses. Additionally, without reliable data for week
371	                                   17, the data set is restricted to less than 50% of all non-IH games played in a season. This
372	                                   introduces bias into the sample used since a large number of meaningful data points are
373	                                   missing.
374	
375	
376	                                   Conclusions
377	                                   The current study investigated the link between game importance and concussion incidence.
378	                                   Overall, concussion incidence does not appear to be affected by the playoff implications
379	                                   associated with each game. However, at the position-specific level, RBs are more likely to suffer
380	                                   a concussion in an IH game than in a non-IH one. This study also confirmed the number of
381	                                   plays per game influences concussion incidence. Future research should expand on this study
382	                                   with a more comprehensive dataset including concussions from week 17 and explore the
383	                                   interaction between plays per game and other known concussion modulators such as the style
384	                                   of play and strength of schedule.

                                         The Effect of Game Importance on
                                         Concussion Incidence in the National
                                         Football League: An Observational Study
                                         Theodore Hannah 1 , Nickolas Dreher 1 , Dhruv S. Shankar 2 , Adam Y. Li 2 , Jennifer Dai 2 , Mark
                                         R. Lovell 3 , Tanvir F. Choudhri 2


                                         1. Neurological Surgery, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, USA 2. Neurological
                                         Surgery, The Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, USA 3. Neurology, University of
                                         Pittsburgh Medical Center, Pittsburgh , USA


                                          Corresponding author: Theodore Hannah, theodore.hannah@icahn.mssm.edu




                                         Abstract
                                         Introduction
                                         Concussion incidence in the National Football League (NFL) has been shown to generally
                                         increase as the season progresses. Yet, there is evidence that suggests that the incidence
                                         stagnates or decreases in the final quarter of the season in comparison to the third quarter. This
                                         anomaly cannot be explained by any of the known modulators of concussion incidence.
                                         However, the fact that the teams start getting eliminated from playoff contention in the fourth
                                         quarter of the season may explain this pattern in concussion incidence. This study tests
                                         whether there is a difference in concussion incidence in games between teams who are still in
                                         the playoff hunt [in the hunt (IH) games] versus games where both teams have had their playoff
                                         fate already determined (non-IH games).


                                         Methods
                                         We obtained details of 166 documented concussions from weeks 13-16 of each of the four NFL
                                         seasons from 2012 to 2015 from Public Broadcasting Service's (PBS) Frontline Concussion Watch
                                         and matched them to the games in which they occurred. Each game was categorized based on
                                         the playoff status [clinched (CL), eliminated (EL), or IH] of the teams playing in the game.
                                         Concussion incidence of the game types was compared to each other using a one-way analysis
                                         of variance (ANOVA) test and student t-tests. Additionally, concussion incidences at six
                                         different player positions in important games were compared to the corresponding incidences
                                         in unimportant games. An ordinary least squares regression was used to examine the effects of
                                         game importance and plays per game on concussion incidence.

                                   Categories: Neurosurgery, Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation
                                   Keywords: football, concussion, national football league (nfl), head injuries, traumatic brain injury
                                   (tbi), sports medicine, american football


                                   Introduction
                                   Incidents of sports injuries have been shown to increase over the course of a game and over the
                                   course of a season [1-5]. This trend is often attributed to player fatigue. However, in the
                                   National Football League (NFL), there are previous reports of no change or a slight decrease in
                                   the incidence of some injuries, including concussions, from the third quarter (weeks 8-12) to
                                   the fourth quarter of the season (weeks 13-16) [1,6]. This stagnation of concussion incidence in
                                   the fourth quarter of the season is inconsistent with the cumulative fatigue hypothesis and
                                   cannot be explained by any of the other known modulators of NFL concussion incidence such as
                                   the strength of schedule, style of play, altitude, temperature, or dew point [7,8]. A novel
                                   modulator is necessary to explain this anomaly.


                                   Studies have shown that a subject’s willingness to endure pain is modulated by the magnitude
                                   of the reward they expect to receive [9-13]. NFL players, having years of experience in making
                                   and receiving hits, are likely to be acutely aware as to which types of plays lead to which type of
                                   hits and which type of hits incur the most pain. Thus, players may modify their exposure to
                                   pain in accordance with their reward valuation of winning a game, and these adjustments in a
                                   player’s willingness to risk injury might modulate the incidence of concussion.


                                   The present study explores whether there is evidence to conclude that individual players
                                   increase their exposure to injury in games with playoff implications. Specifically, it tests the
                                   hypothesis that the concussion incidence is higher in games between teams who are still in the
                                   playoff hunt [in the hunt (IH) games] than in games where both teams have had their playoff
                                   fate already determined (non-IH games).


                                   Materials And Methods
                                   Data collection
                                   The total number of wins accrued by each of the 32 NFL teams prior to weeks 13-16 of each of
                                   the 2012-2015 NFL seasons (four years) were collected from archived data from the NFL [14].
                                   The number of wins of each team prior to each week’s games was used to sort the teams into
                                   three categories: IH, eliminated (EL), and clinched (CL). Teams were considered EL when they
                                   could no longer win enough games to be first in their division or catch the team in the second
                                   position in the wild-card race in their conference. Teams were considered to be CL if no other
                                   team in their division could match their wins or if they were in a top-two position in the wild-
                                   card race in their conference and the third-place team in the wildcard race could not match
                                   their wins. All other teams were assigned to the IH category.


                                   Concussions occurring during the preseason or playoffs were excluded. Week 17 was also
                                   excluded because teams were not required to report concussions from that week if their team
                                   did not make the playoffs [15]. Analyses were restricted to weeks 13-16 after determining it was
                                   exceedingly rare for a team to be mathematically eliminated prior to week 13. Concussion data
                                   for weeks 13-16 of the 2012-2015 regular seasons were taken from Public Broadcasting Service's
                                   (PBS) Frontline Concussion Watch [16]. Frontline gives the following information about each
                                   concussion: player injured, player position, player team, number of games missed following the
                                   injury, and the week of the season the concussion was reported. All concussions were assumed



2019 Hannah et al. Cureus 11(11): e6252. DOI 10.7759/cureus.6252                                                                       2 of 10
                                    to have occurred during games, although this is not always the case [2]. Each concussion (n =
                                   166) was matched to the game (n = 256) with which it was associated.


                                   Based on the classification of the teams playing (IH, EL, CL), each game was sorted into one of
                                   6 categories: IH versus IH (IH v IH), IH versus CL (IH v CL), IH versus EL (IH v EL), CL versus CL
                                   (CL v CL), CL versus EL (CL v EL), and EL versus EL (EL v EL). The number of games in each
                                   category was as follows: IH v IH: 161, IH v CL: 17, IH v EL: 51, CL v CL: 4, CL v EL: 8, and EL v
                                   EL: 15. For analyses involving the fourth category, crucial (CR), teams that would have been
                                   sorted into the IH category were instead considered CR if they would be eliminated from playoff
                                   contention (as described above) should they not win that week’s game. This added four more
                                   game types: IH versus CR (IH v CR), CL versus CR (CL v CR), EL versus CR (EL v CR), and CR
                                   versus CR (CR v CR). And the number of games in each category was as follows: IH v CR:39, CL
                                   v CR: 4, EL v CR: 17, and CR v CR: 5. The adjusted number of games in each category was: IH v
                                   CR: 39, CL v CR: 4, EL v CR: 17, CR v CR: 5, IH v IH: 117, IH v CL: 13, IH v EL: 34, CL v CL: 4, CL
                                   v EL: 8, and EL v EL: 15.


                                   For our position-specific analyses, concussion incidence at six positions was individually
                                   compared in IH games to non-IH games using the same protocol as described above. The
                                   positions analyzed were wide receivers (WR), running backs (RB), tight ends (TE), quarterbacks
                                   (QB), safeties (SA), and cornerbacks (CB). The corresponding number of concussions over 256
                                   games was: 17 for WR, 13 for RB, 21 for TE, 5 for QB, 16 for SA, and 30 for CB.


                                   Concussions per game for all analyses were calculated using the formula: number of
                                   concussions in relevant games/number of relevant games. Plays per game data were pulled
                                   from the sports data website TeamRankings (www.teamrankings.com) [17]. Plays per game were
                                   defined as the sum of total offensive plays for both teams reported by the TeamRankings
                                   website. Temperature and dew point data were taken from NFLWeather (www.nflweather.com)
                                   [18]. NFL stadium altitude data was obtained through ArcGIS NFL Stadium Elevation [19].


                                   Data analysis
                                   Data analysis was performed with Prism 8 (GraphPad, San Diego, CA). In accordance with
                                   statistical best practices to handle large differences in variance, all t-tests and one-way
                                   analyses of variance (ANOVA) were performed with Welch’s correction [20]. For all analyses,
                                   including correlations, t-tests, ANOVAs, and multilinear regressions, statistical significance
                                   was defined as α = 0.05. Mean values are presented with the standard error of the mean (SEM).


                                   Regression analysis
                                   A multivariate regression analysis to explain the number of concussions per games was
                                   performed using environmental variables known to affect concussions (altitude, temperature,
                                   and dew point), plays per game, and a dummy variable for importance of the game (IH dummy;
                                   1 if at least one IH team is playing; 0 otherwise). The general form of the regression was:
                                   concussions = β0 + β1IH dummy + β2total plays + β3altitude + β4temperature + β5dew point.


                                   Results
                                   IH games (mean = 0.651 ±0.055) and non-IH games (mean = 0.623 ±0.143) were found to have
                                   similar concussion incidence (p: 0.890, Figure 1A). Concussion incidence was not significantly
                                   different between the six game types (IH v IH, IH v CL, IH v EL, CL v CL, CL v EL, and El v EL)
                                   [F(5,250): 0.693, p: 0.625], but there was a trend when teams in the same category play each
                                   other. Specifically, CL v CL games had the lowest concussion incidence (mean = 0.250 ±0.250)
                                   whereas EL v EL (mean = 0.600 ±0.1902) and IH v IH (mean = 0.6211 ±0.0623) games were both
                                   higher than CL v CL and similar in magnitude to each other (Figure 1B). Due to the non-



2019 Hannah et al. Cureus 11(11): e6252. DOI 10.7759/cureus.6252                                                                 3 of 10
                                    significant results, the correlation between the number of plays per game and the concussion
                                   incidence was assessed. The correlation coefficient was positive and significant (r: 0.3578, p:
                                   0.0054), but was moderate in magnitude (Figure 1C). We also found no significant differences
                                   in the average number of plays per game between the game types [F(5,250): 0.925, p: 0.466].

                                     per game. All error bars represent SEM. No significant differences are present in either Figure 1A or

                                   To account for possible effects of a team being "pseudo-eliminated" (one loss away from playoff
                                   elimination), a new team category, CR, was created. However, even with this exclusion
                                   modification (Figure 2A), there was no statistical difference (p: 0.766) between games with at
                                   least one IH team (mean = 0.677 ±0.066) and games with only CL or EL teams (mean = 0.630

                                    ±0.143). When these categories are broken down into specific game types (Figure 2C), no

                                   incidence in games involving teams of the same category remained consistent (Figure 2B), with
                                   IH v IH games having the highest incidence (mean = 0.675 ±0.072), followed by EL v EL (mean =
                                   0.600 ±0.190), CR v CR (mean = 0.400 ±0.245), and then CL v CL (mean = 0.250 ±0.250).

                                     number of concussions for all subdivided game types. All error bars represent SEM. No significant
                                     differences are present in Figure 2


                                     CL: clinched; EL: eliminated; IH: in the hunt; v: versus; SEM: standard error of the mean




                                   Next, concussion incidence at a number of player positions during IH and non-IH games was
                                   examined. Figure 3B shows that RBs have significantly higher incidence of concussion (p:
                                   0.004) in IH games (mean = 0.049 ±0.0170) compared to non-IH games (mean = 0.00 ±0.00) TEs
                                   appeared to follow this trend as well (IH mean = 0.092 ±0.0227, non-IH mean = 0.03571



2019 Hannah et al. Cureus 11(11): e6252. DOI 10.7759/cureus.6252                                                                     5 of 10
                                    ±0.0357), although the difference did not reach statistical significance (p: 0.189). WRs, QBs,
                                   SAs, and CBs all showed no difference in concussion incidence based on game importance.




                                     FIGURE 3: Position-specific effects of games with playoff
                                     implications
                                     The number of concussions per game across six different positions in games where at least one
                                     team is in the playoff hunt (IH) versus games with no teams in the hunt (non-IH). All error bars
                                     represent SEM


                                     QB: quarterback; WR: wide receiver; CB: cornerback; TE: tight end; SA: safety; RB: running
                                     back; SEM: standard error of the mean




                                   Finally, a regression analysis was performed using environmental modulators of concussion
                                   incidence, plays per game, and the importance of the game (Table 1). The results showed that
                                   the importance of the game does not significantly influence concussion incidence (p: 0.794),
                                   but plays per game do (p: 0.025), even when accounting for known environmental modulators.
                                   In this model, games with 10 more plays increased the number of concussions per game by 0.16.

                                     Discussion
                                     To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study that has investigated the relationship
                                     between the importance of a game and concussion incidence. Surprisingly, the results suggest
                                     that, except for RBs, players are not more likely to suffer concussions in games with playoff
                                     implications than in games without. Instead, a major modulator of concussion risk is the
                                     number of plays per game [21].


                                     Previous research has shown that TEs, RBs, CBs, and WRs have the highest rates of concussion,
                                     and passing positions overall have higher concussion incidence than running plays. This is
                                     attributed to the nature of collisions that occur in passing positions [1,22]. RBs did have higher
                                     concussion incidence in IH games, but contrary to expectations, the same effect was absent for
                                     TEs, CBs, and WRs. Due to the low sample size, further research will be necessary to validate
                                     and explain this phenomenon. However, one explanation is that there may be differences in
                                     fatigue and risk exposure inherent in various positions. For example, even though teams tend
                                     to throw the ball more often than they run it, an individual RB gets more touches per game than
                                     an individual receiver, increasing fatigue for the RB [7]. Furthermore, RBs get hit almost every
                                     time they touch the ball, increasing their exposure to concussion risk, whereas an individual
                                     WR gets fewer targets per game and gets hit on a lower percentage of those plays due to the
                                     prevailing rates of incomplete passes.


                                     The hypothesis for higher concussion incidence in IH games is predicated on the idea that
                                     players make riskier plays and/or increase the force of their tackles to increase their team’s
                                     chances of winning. The lack of significant differences both overall and at individual positions
                                     may be due to the naturally high-velocity impacts experienced at those positions accompanied
                                     by the highest concussion incidence. A previous study on concussion biomechanics
                                     demonstrated that a different concussion risk modulator, improved helmet manufacturing, can
                                     decrease concussion incidence for 16.6 mph and 20.8 mph impacts; however, for high-velocity
                                     impacts of 25.1 mph, the same improved helmet technology had zero effect on concussion
                                     incidence [23]. Since the player positions most vulnerable to concussion are also experiencing
                                     the highest velocity impacts, it may be more difficult for players to modulate their risk exposure



2019 Hannah et al. Cureus 11(11): e6252. DOI 10.7759/cureus.6252                                                                          7 of 10
                                    than previously expected.


                                   There were a few assumptions made in this study that, if untrue, may explain why the
                                   importance of the game does not appear to modulate concussion incidence. The first is that the
                                   effect of game importance on concussion incidence would be modulated solely through
                                   modifications that players make at the individual level. However, a previous study had
                                   concluded that a team’s style of play influenced concussion incidence [7]. Certain coaching
                                   styles may limit an individual player’s ability to modulate their exposure to concussion-
                                   inducing collisions. With a larger dataset, further stratification of games across the offensive
                                   and defensive styles of play of each team would likely be a valuable investigation. It was also
                                   assumed that the importance of the game to the team’s playoff hopes would be the single
                                   element of influence on how inclined a player would be to risk injury to improve their team’s
                                   chances of winning. However, players who are in the last year of their contract may be
                                   motivated to demonstrate their full potential irrespective of team standings. Moreover, when
                                   games become unimportant from a playoff standpoint, coaches may give second and third-
                                   string players opportunities to showcase their abilities to management to increase their stock
                                   for the following year. These players are much more likely to risk injury to prove their
                                   worth. Finally, all players were assumed to have an equal ability to adjust their games to reduce
                                   their risk of injury. It has been previously shown that players with lesser skills suffer
                                   concussions more frequently than more skilled players [24,25]. If players with lesser skills are
                                   less able to mitigate concussion risk but receive more playing time in non-IH games, this would
                                   dampen any effect of the skilled players avoiding concussions in non-IH games.


                                   Limitations
                                   In addition to the limitations inherent in these assumptions, this study is also limited by low
                                   sample size in many of the game-type categories of interest, leading to unequal variances
                                   between groups. A study that involves more seasons with reliable concussion data would
                                   improve the accuracy and power of these analyses. Additionally, without reliable data for week
                                   17, the data set is restricted to less than 50% of all non-IH games played in a season. This
                                   introduces bias into the sample used since a large number of meaningful data points are
                                   missing.


                                   Conclusions
                                   The current study investigated the link between game importance and concussion incidence.
                                   Overall, concussion incidence does not appear to be affected by the playoff implications
                                   associated with each game. However, at the position-specific level, RBs are more likely to suffer
                                   a concussion in an IH game than in a non-IH one. This study also confirmed the number of
                                   plays per game influences concussion incidence. Future research should expand on this study
                                   with a more comprehensive dataset including concussions from week 17 and explore the
                                   interaction between plays per game and other known concussion modulators such as the style
                                   of play and strength of schedule.

J Appl Physiol 138: 1150–1160, 2025.
First published April 7, 2025; doi:10.1152/japplphysiol.01004.2024



 RESEARCH ARTICLE

The effect of heat acclimation on critical environmental limits and rate of rectal
temperature change
           Timo van den Bogaard,1 Lisa Klous,2               Rachel M. Cottle,3            Jan Van Erp,2,4 and            Hein A. M. Daanen1
       1
        Department of Human Movement Sciences, Faculty of Behavioural and Movement Sciences, Amsterdam Movement
       Sciences, Vrije Universiteit van Amsterdam, Amsterdam, The Netherlands; 2Department of Human Performance, Netherlands
       Organization for Applied Scientiﬁc Research (TNO), Unit Defence, Safety and Security, Soesterberg, The Netherlands;
       3
         Department of Kinesiology, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania, United States; and 4Department
       Human Media Interaction, Faculty Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Twente,
       Enschede, The Netherlands

Abstract
Quantifying the effect of heat acclimation (HA) on critical wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGTcrit) and rate of rectal temperature change
(vTre) is relevant for developing guidelines with regards to occupational safety while working in warm environments. This study quantiﬁed
the effect of HA and the period following cessation of the HA protocol on WBGTcrit and vTre. Twenty-eight non-acclimatized participants
were divided into a HA (n ¼ 15) and control (CON; n ¼ 13) group. The HA group underwent a warm-humid (35 C, 65% relative humidity)
controlled hyperthermia HA protocol (5–9 days of achieving Tre 38.5 C for 60 min) and four progressive heat stress tests (HSTs) to
identify WBGTcrit and examine vTre: pre-, after 5 and 9 days of HA, and 4 to 8 days of no heat exposure following HA. CON performed
two HSTs on average 13 days apart without heat exposure in between. HA increased WBGTcrit after nine (28.5 ± 2.7 C vs. 30.5 ± 2.0 C;
P ¼ 0.016) but not 5 days (28.5 ± 2.4; P > 0.05). No effect of HA on vTre was observed (P > 0.05). Four-to-eight days post-HA,
WBGTcrit and vTre did not differ compared with 9 days of HA (P > 0.05). However, a reduction in vTre (0.4 ± 0.3  C/h) was observed
when comparing 4 to 8 days post-HA to pre-HA. In conclusion, our results demonstrate that more than 5 days of HA are required to

 "evidenceSummary":"Controlled, non-randomized laboratory study in 28 healthy, unacclimatized, regularly active adults (heat acclimation group n = 15, control n = 13) using a 9-day controlled-hyperthermia cycling protocol and progressive heat stress tests. Critical wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGTcrit) rose by 2.3 ± 2.7 C WBGT after 9 days but not after 5 days, and the rise was still present 4 to 8 days after the protocol stopped. The rate of rectal temperature rise did not change during heat acclimation, but within the acclimation group it was lower 4 to 8 days after cessation than at baseline.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Groups were allocated by availability rather than randomly, and WBGTcrit could not be identified in many tests, so the key between-group analysis included only 7 acclimation and 6 control participants.  "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the 4 to 8 day post-protocol drop in rectal temperature rise as a proven benefit of recovery after acclimation, when it was a within-group change with no control comparison at that time point and may partly reflect a change in starting temperature.",

   "citation":"van den Bogaard T, Klous L, Cottle RM, Van Erp J, Daanen HAM. The effect of heat acclimation on critical environmental limits and rate of rectal temperature change. J Appl Physiol. 2025;138:1150-1160.",
   "doi":"10.1152/japplphysiol.01004.2024",
   "abstract":"The study quantified how heat acclimation changes the critical environmental limit (WBGTcrit, the point where heat balance can no longer be maintained) and the rate of rectal temperature rise during exercise in the heat. Twenty-eight unacclimatized adults were split into a heat acclimation group, which completed 5 to 9 days of controlled-hyperthermia cycling in 35 C and 65% humidity, and a control group. WBGTcrit increased after 9 but not 5 days, and rectal temperature rise was only reduced 4 to 8 days after the protocol ended.",
   "tldr":"In active adults, 9 days of controlled-hyperthermia heat acclimation raised the heat level they could tolerate before core temperature kept climbing, but 5 days did not. The gain was still present 4 to 8 days after heat exposure stopped.",
   "methods":"Participants (heat acclimation 6 men and 9 women; control 6 men and 7 women; VO2max about 46 mL/kg/min) were matched on body mass, VO2max, sex, age and body surface area and allocated by available time. The acclimation group completed progressive heat stress tests (cycling at fixed heat production in 38 C with stepwise rising humidity) before, after 5 and 9 days of acclimation, and after 4 or 8 days without heat; controls completed two tests about 13 days apart. WBGTcrit was set by visual inspection of the rectal temperature curve, and analyses used mixed-model and repeated-measures ANOVA.",
   "findings":"WBGTcrit showed a group by time interaction (P = 0.016), rising from 28.5 to 30.5 C WBGT after 9 days in the acclimation group with no change after 5 days. The rate of rectal temperature rise showed no group by time interaction (P = 0.537); within the acclimation group it was lower 4 to 8 days after cessation than at baseline (0.6 versus 0.9 C/h). After 9 days, sweat loss rose by 165 mL/h and starting rectal temperature fell by 0.44 C relative to controls, and only starting rectal temperature showed decay after cessation.",
   "limitations":"Visual identification of WBGTcrit left many missing values, so only 6 to 7 acclimation participants contributed to the key analyses, and an objective segmented-regression method did not reproduce the visual result (r = 0.33). Groups were not randomized, rectal temperature responds slowly, and 9 days may not be the minimum effective dose. Controls also showed unexplained drops in skin temperature and heart rate between tests.",
   "practicalImplications":"With a controlled-hyperthermia protocol in warm-humid conditions, 5 days of heat acclimation did not raise the critical heat limit, while 9 days did. A short gap of 4 to 8 days without heat exposure after acclimation did not erase the WBGTcrit gain in this sample.",
   "athleteDev":"For athletes preparing for hot competition or preseason, the data suggest planning more than 5 days of controlled-hyperthermia heat sessions if the goal is a higher heat tolerance limit. The sample was active adults rather than athletes, so magnitudes may differ in trained athletes.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions after injury or heat illness. It measured heat tolerance in healthy adults and did not study recovery from exertional heat illness."

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW



The Effect of Pre‑Exercise Hyperhydration on Exercise Performance,
Physiological Outcomes and Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Systematic
Review
William T. Jardine1 · Brad Aisbett1 · Monica K. Kelly1 · Louise M. Burke2              · Megan L. Ross2     ·
Dominique Condo1 · Julien D. Périard3 · Amelia J. Carr1

Accepted: 19 June 2023
© The Author(s) 2023


Abstract
Background Fluid loss during prolonged exercise in hot conditions poses thermoregulatory and cardiovascular challenges
for athletes that can lead to impaired performance. Pre-exercise hyperhydration using nutritional aids is a strategy that may
prevent or delay the adverse effects of dehydration and attenuate the impact of heat stress on exercise performance.
Objectives The aim of this systematic review was to examine the current literature to determine the effect of pre-exercise
hyperhydration on performance, key physiological responses and gastrointestinal symptoms.
Methods English language, full-text articles that compared the intervention with a baseline or placebo condition were
included. An electronic search of Medline Complete, SPORTDiscus and Embase were used to identify articles with the
final search conducted on 11 October 2022. Studies were assessed using the American Dietetic Association Quality Criteria
Checklist.
Results Thirty-eight studies involving 403 participants (n = 361 males) were included in this review (n = 22 assessed exer-
cise performance or capacity). Two studies reported an improvement in time-trial performance (range 5.7–11.4%), three
studies reported an improvement in total work completed (kJ) (range 4–5%) and five studies reported an increase in exercise
capacity (range 14.3–26.2%). During constant work rate exercise, nine studies observed a reduced mean heart rate (range
3–11 beats ­min−1), and eight studies reported a reduced mean core temperature (range 0.1–0.8 °C). Ten studies reported
an increase in plasma volume (range 3.5–12.6%) compared with a control. Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 26
studies, with differences in severity potentially associated with factors within the ingestion protocol of each study (e.g. treat-
ment, dose, ingestion rate).
Conclusions Pre-exercise hyperhydration may improve exercise capacity during constant work rate exercise due to a reduced
heart rate and core temperature, stemming from an acute increase in plasma volume. The combination of different osmotic
aids (e.g. glycerol and sodium) may enhance fluid retention and this area should continue to be explored. Future research
should utilise valid and reliable methods of assessing gastrointestinal symptoms. Furthermore, studies should investigate
the effect of hyperhydration on different exercise modalities whilst implementing a strong level of blinding. Finally, females
are vastly underrepresented, and this remains a key area of interest in this area.

498: and found that glycerol hyperhydration improved triathlon
506: time-trial performance by 5.7% compared with placebo on
507: the hotter day [18]. Of the four studies that investigated
508: cycling performance using endurance trained males, three
509: were conducted in laboratory conditions and one in the
510: field. Of the laboratory-based studies, following a 7 day
513: supplementation period of creatine + glycerol [55], or with

{
 "id":"Q68",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of probable COVID-19 infection on the National Football League players performance and endurance during the 2020 season.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in the text, 'The Effect of Probable COVID-19 Infection on the National Football League Players' Performance and Endurance During the 2020 Season', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Performance","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["American Football"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Retrospective single-arm cohort of 78 NFL players who spent at least 10 days on the COVID-19 Injury Reserve list in the 2020 season and played in at least two games before and after. Mean Pro Football Focus score was 62.15 before and 61.73 after infection (p = 0.33), and mean snaps per game was 38.99 before and 38.10 after (p = 0.30). Position-level declines were significant only for defensive backs in snaps (n = 6, down 18.30, p = 0.03) and defensive linemen in PFF score (n = 21, down 3.77, p = 0.03).",
 "screeningLimitations":"This is a small, uncontrolled before-and-after comparison, and the position groups are very small (six defensive backs). PFF score and snap count are proxies for performance and endurance, and the design cannot separate infection effects from injuries, rest or other season changes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the defensive back snap decline as evidence that COVID-19 impairs endurance, when that subgroup has six players and the authors judge the evidence inconclusive overall.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Walker CR, Belisario J, Abramoff B. The Effect of Probable COVID-19 Infection on the National Football League Players' Performance and Endurance During the 2020 Season. Cureus. 2023;15(3):e35821.",
   "doi":"10.7759/cureus.35821",
   "abstract":"The authors asked whether NFL players with probable COVID-19 in the 2020 season showed a drop in performance or endurance. Players who spent at least 10 days on the league's COVID-19 Injury Reserve list and had played in two or more games before and after were compared using snaps per game and PFF score per game. Across all players, neither measure changed significantly, but defensive backs and defensive linemen showed declines.",
   "tldr":"Among 78 NFL players with probable COVID-19 in 2020, overall performance grades and snap counts did not change significantly after infection. Declines in two small position groups need confirmation in larger samples.",
   "methods":"Retrospective single-arm cohort. Players were drawn from the NFL COVID-19 Injury Reserve list (at least 10 days, two or more games either side of listing, offensive or defensive position). Snaps per game and PFF score per game were compared before and after infection with within-group t-tests, overall and by position.",
   "findings":"PFF score fell from 62.15 to 61.73 (decrease 0.42, p = 0.33) and snaps per game fell from 38.99 to 38.10 (decrease 0.89, p = 0.30) across 78 players. Defensive backs (n = 6) lost 18.30 snaps per game (p = 0.03) and defensive linemen (n = 21) lost 3.77 PFF points (p = 0.03). The authors judge the evidence inconclusive for other positions and for all players combined.",
   "limitations":"Confounders such as injuries to the player or teammates, trades, weekly game strategy, opponent difficulty and officiating were not analysed. Position groups were small, and infection status was inferred from injury-reserve listing rather than medical records, so symptomatic and asymptomatic cases could not be separated. The study also could not distinguish infection effects from extra rest before return.",
   "practicalImplications":"Across the group, performance and snap counts did not change clearly after probable COVID-19. The defensive back and defensive lineman signals suggest staff should track snap counts and performance grades after a player returns from infection, and treat these results as hypotheses to test.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports monitoring snap counts and performance grades after a player returns from COVID-19, with particular attention to defensive backs and linemen. It does not show that all players lose output.",
   "rtp":"The study does not address medical clearance or safe timing for return to play after COVID-19. It measured in-season output only and cannot set return criteria."
 }
}

21	
22	
23	
24	                                                Abstract
25	                                                Objective
26	                                                The objective of this study was to assess whether the National Football League (NFL) players with probable
27	                                                coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) during the 2020 season experienced a decline in athletic performance
28	                                                and endurance.
29	
30	
31	                                                Methods
32	                                                All players who were listed on the NFL’s COVID-19 Injury Reserve (COVID-IR) list were screened for
33	                                                inclusion. Players were included in the study if they had spent ≥10 days on the COVID-19 IR list (which
34	                                                indicated a positive PCR test based on the NFL COVID-19 policies), had played in at least two games before
35	                                                and after going on the IR list, and primarily played an offensive or defensive position. The mean number of
36	                                                snaps played per game and Pro Football Focus (PFF) score per game were collected for each athlete, which
37	                                                served as surrogate measures of endurance and performance, respectively. The results were analyzed with
38	                                                players grouped by position, and then all players grouped as a whole. Within-group comparisons were
39	                                                performed via t-tests.
40	
41	
42	                                                Results
43	                                                A total of 78 players met the criteria for inclusion in the study. The overall mean PFF score pre-COVID-19
44	                                                infection was 62.15 (SD: 6.93), while it was 61.73 (SD: 7.42) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of
45	                                                0.42 after infection (n=78, p=0.33). The mean number of snaps played per game pre-COVID-19 infection was
46	                                                38.99 (SD: 16.46) while it was 38.10 (SD: 17.05) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of 0.89 after
47	                                                infection (n=78, p=0.30). When grouped by position, statistically significant differences were seen with
48	                                                Defensive Backs’ mean snaps played per game decreasing by 18.30 (n=6, p=0.03) and Defensive Linemen’s
49	                                                mean PFF score decreasing by 3.77 points (n=21, p=0.03).
50	
51	
52	                                                Conclusion
53	                                                Based on our findings, COVID-19 infection negatively impacted endurance in Defensive Backs, and
54	                                                performance in Defensive Linemen. However, there was inconclusive evidence to show whether COVID-19
55	                                                infection negatively impacted other positions when analyzed separately or all positions when analyzed
56	                                                together. Further studies with more participants are needed to fully assess the effects of COVID-19 on
57	                                                performance and endurance in elite athletes.
58	
59	
60	
61	                                                Categories: Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, Infectious Disease, Orthopedics
62	                                                Keywords: physical medicine and rehabilitation (pm&r), sports medicine, performance, endurance, athletes, nfl,
63	                                                football, covid-19
64	
65	
66	
67	                                                Introduction
68	                                                As the world struggled to balance normalcy with safety amidst the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)
69	                                                pandemic, many professional sports leagues reopened in the United States prior to vaccines against the
70	                                                disease becoming available. One of the earliest examples, the National Football League (NFL), was able to
71	                                                complete the 2020-2021 season after implementing rigorous testing and isolation protocols, including the
72	                                                administration of over 600,000 COVID-19 tests over the six-month season [1].
73	
74	
75	                                                Through these protocols, the NFL was generally able to mitigate large outbreaks, although individual players
76	                                                still tested positive for the virus. A recent meta-analysis found that acute symptoms are mild or absent in
77	                                                ~94% of athletes, but 3.8-17% will go on to develop persistent symptoms that may be detrimental to their
78	                                                performance [2]. This is in line with anecdotal reports of some NFL players experiencing a longer duration of
79	                                                symptoms leading to diminished on-field performance. Myles Garrett, a two-time NFL All-Pro Defensive
80	                                                End for the Cleveland Browns, was outspoken about his post-COVID-19 sequela. He was on the COVID-19
81	
82	
83	                               How to cite this article
84	                               Walker C R, Belisario J, Abramoff B (March 06, 2023) The Effect of Probable COVID-19 Infection on the National Football League Players’
85	                               Performance and Endurance During the 2020 Season. Cureus 15(3): e35821. DOI 10.7759/cureus.35821
86	                                                  Injury Reserve (COVID-IR) list for 11 days. Following this, he reported that he felt he was operating at 50%
87	                                                 and that fatigue prevented him from performing at his best for extended periods of time [3]. Similar stories
88	                                                 from other notable professional athletes have been reported, including Jayson Tatum, a three-time National
89	                                                 Basketball Association (NBA) All-Star who currently plays for the Boston Celtics, and Yoan Moncada who
90	                                                 plays second base for the Chicago White Sox of Major League Baseball (MLB) [4,5].
91	
92	
93	                                                 The objective of this study was to evaluate the performance of NFL players before and after a presumed
94	                                                 positive test for COVID-19 during the 2020-2021 NFL season.
95	
96	
97	                                                 Materials And Methods
98	                                                 Study design
99	                                                 We adopted a retrospective single-arm cohort study design, using individual player data to compare
100	                                                 performance and endurance pre-COVID-19 infection to performance and endurance post-COVID-19
101	                                                 infection. The study was deemed exempt by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board.
102	
103	
104	                                                 Participants
105	                                                 During the 2020-2021 season, the NFL created a COVID-IR list. This list included players who tested positive
106	                                                 or had close-contact exposure to someone with COVID-19. Following a high-risk exposure, a player could
107	                                                 return to team activities after having two negative tests within 24 hours. Following a positive test, an
108	                                                 asymptomatic player could return to team activities after 10 days since the initial positive test or if he tested
109	                                                 negative twice at least 24 hours apart. If the player was symptomatic, he could return to team activities after
110	                                                 10 days from the time symptoms first appeared and after 24 hours since he last experienced symptoms [6].
111	                                                 For the purposes of this study, a player was considered to have a COVID-19 infection if they were placed on
112	                                                 the COVID-19 IR list during the 2020-2021 season and were on the list for 10 days or more. Since vaccines
113	                                                 for COVID-19 were not available during the study period, all participants were considered unvaccinated.
114	
115	
116	                                                 To exclude players who were placed on the COVID-19 IR list due to high-risk exposure, we excluded any
117	                                                 player who was on the COVID-19 IR list for less than 10 days. We also excluded players who played in fewer
118	                                                 than two games either before testing positive or after they returned, to allow for averaging of their
119	                                                 performance and endurance across multiple games. We also excluded Special Teams players due to the
120	                                                 limited data available to determine on-field performance.
121	
122	
123	                                                 All NFL players listed on the NFL’s COVID-IR list during the 2020-2021 season were screened for inclusion.
124	
125	
126	                                                 Data collection and analysis
127	                                                 To assess athletic performance, we compared the mean Pro Football Focus (PFF) score per game pre- and
128	                                                 post-COVID-19 infection. PFF is a commonly used grading system that evaluates individual players based on
129	                                                 their overall performance in a game. To calculate a player’s PFF score, a panel of professional analysts
130	                                                 assigns each player a score from -2 to 2 in 0.5 increments for every play that they are on the field for with 0
131	                                                 being the average or “expected” score. A senior analyst will review all the grades, finalize them, then convert
132	                                                 the plus-minus grades to an overall score for the game, ranging from 0 to 100, with 0 being the worst and 100
133	                                                 being the best. PFF evaluates player performance in a standardized manner across all positions, allowing for
134	                                                 direct comparison [7]. Overall game scores were collected for every player who met the inclusion criteria.
135	                                                 These scores were then averaged pre- and post-COVID-19 infection for comparison.
136	
137	
138	                                                 The publicly available number of “snaps” (plays) that each player participated in was used as a proxy of
139	                                                 player endurance. The overall number of “snaps” that players participated in per game was collected for
140	                                                 every player who met the inclusion criteria. The number of snaps played per game was then averaged pre-
141	                                                 and post-COVID-19 infection for comparison.
142	
143	
144	                                                 Analysis was done for the whole group and by position. Within-group comparisons were performed using t-
145	                                                 tests. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
146	
147	
148	                                                 Results
149	                                                 A total of 368 players were placed on the COVID-IR list during the season due to high-risk exposures or a
150	                                                 positive PCR test; 78 of the 368 players met the criteria for probable COVID-19 infection and were included
151	                                                 in our analysis. The overall mean PFF score pre-COVID-19 infection was 62.15 (SD: 6.93), while it was 61.73
152	                                                 (SD: 7.42) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of 0.42 after infection (n=78, p=0.33, range: -20.55
153	                                                 to 18.18). The mean number of snaps played per game pre-COVID-19 infection was 38.99 (SD: 16.46), while
154	                                                 it was 38.10 (SD: 17.05) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of 0.89 after infection (n=78, p=0.30,
155	                                                 range: -48.83 to 49.68).
156	
157	
158	                                                 When grouped by position, a statistically significant decrease in the mean PFF score was seen among
159	                                                 Defensive Linemen (mean decrease: 3.77, n=21, p=0.03). A decrease in mean PFF score was also seen among
160	
161	
162	
163	2023 Walker et al. Cureus 15(3): e35821. DOI 10.7759/cureus.35821                                                                                                    2 of 6
164	                                                         Tight Ends (mean decrease: 4.12, n=6, p=0.10) and Offensive Linemen (mean decrease: 0.43, n=10, p=0.42).

253	                                                 Discussion
254	                                                 COVID-19 is a viral illness that infiltrates the body via the respiratory tract [8]. It can cause direct cellular
255	                                                 damage to the lung parenchyma as well as systemic damage by triggering a cytokine storm [9]. Through the
256	                                                 systemic inflammatory process, COVID-19 can cause myocarditis, pericarditis, or direct myocardial injury
257	                                                 [10]. The data regarding the prevalence of myocardial abnormalities after COVID-19 infection in the athlete
258	                                                 population varies considerably but is thought to be around 5% [2]. Due to the concern for sudden cardiac
259	                                                 death, extensive screening is recommended by the American College of Cardiology for athletes with severe
260	                                                 or persistent symptoms prior to returning to sport [11]. Even after being medically cleared to return to sport,
261	                                                 some athletes feel lingering symptoms that subjectively impact their performance, which this study
262	                                                 attempts to quantify [1-6,12].
263	
264	
265	                                                 Although a decrease in the mean PFF score and the mean number of snaps played after the COVID-19
266	                                                 infection was found when looking at all players, these were neither statically significant nor very large in
267	                                                 magnitude. However, when analyzed by position, there was a statistically significant decrease in the mean
268	                                                 number of snaps played by Defensive Backs and a statistically significant decrease in Defensive Linemen’s
269	                                                 mean PFF score. Other positions also showed trends that were approaching statistical significance (e.g.,
270	                                                 Tight Ends’ decrease in PFF score and Running Backs’ increase in PFF score).
271	
272	
273	                                                 The variability in outcomes may be due to the wide range of symptoms experienced by those with COVID-19
274	                                                 infection and the heterogeneity of the positions played by the athletes and their unique physical demands.
275	                                                 For example, Defensive Backs experience fewer high-energy collisions but run more than any other position
276	                                                 on defense, covering about 3 miles per game [13,14]. Given the endurance component of their position
277	                                                 compared to other defensive positions, this may explain why this group saw a statistically significant
278	                                                 decrease in the mean number of snaps per game after returning from COVID-19 infection while other
279	                                                 positions did not. Defensive Linemen, alternatively, had a statically significant decrease in their mean PFF
280	                                                 score after returning from COVID-19. This group had the highest BMI of all the defensive players, at 36.31
281	                                                 kg/m2. Obesity has been correlated with worse COVID-19 symptoms, which may explain this trend [15].
282	                                                 Running Backs, who sustain the greatest number of severe impacts (>10 G force) per game, had an increase
283	                                                 in mean PFF score that approached statical significance [13]. We hypothesize that the time away from sport
284	                                                 allowed them to better recover from the intense physical demands of their position and thus perform better
285	                                                 upon returning.
286	
287	
288	                                                 Limitations
289	                                                 There are numerous confounding factors that exist within an NFL season that may impact an individual
290	                                                 player’s PFF score or number of snaps played, none of which were able to be analyzed in our study. A few
291	                                                 examples of confounding factors are injuries to the players or their teammates, trades between teams
292	                                                 involving the players or their teammates, different game strategies used on a weekly basis, changes in the
293	                                                 difficulty of the opposition on a weekly basis, and differences in refereeing by in-game officials. Our study
294	                                                 was further limited by the small number of players that met the inclusion criteria for each position and by
295	                                                 not having access to NFL testing data and official medical history for the players. Hence, COVID-19-positive
296	                                                 cases were deduced using the NFL isolation protocol and the amount of time players spent on the COVID-IR
297	                                                 list, which may have resulted in excluding some true positive cases and failing to differentiate asymptomatic
298	                                                 cases from symptomatic cases. Lastly, it was impossible to distinguish performance changes due to COVID-
299	                                                 19 infection vs. changes due to the athlete having several days of rest before returning to sport.
300	
301	
302	                                                 Conclusions
303	                                                 Based on our findings, probable COVID-19 infection negatively impacted endurance among Defensive
304	                                                 Backs, and performance among Defensive Linemen. However, the evidence was inconclusive as to whether
305	                                                 COVID-19 infection negatively impacted other positions when analyzed separately or all positions when
306	                                                 analyzed together. Further studies with more participants are warranted to gain deeper insights into the
307	                                                 effects of COVID-19 on performance and endurance among professional American football athletes.
