                                                Abstract
                                                Objective
                                                The objective of this study was to assess whether the National Football League (NFL) players with probable
                                                coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) during the 2020 season experienced a decline in athletic performance
                                                and endurance.


                                                Methods
                                                All players who were listed on the NFL’s COVID-19 Injury Reserve (COVID-IR) list were screened for
                                                inclusion. Players were included in the study if they had spent ≥10 days on the COVID-19 IR list (which
                                                indicated a positive PCR test based on the NFL COVID-19 policies), had played in at least two games before
                                                and after going on the IR list, and primarily played an offensive or defensive position. The mean number of
                                                snaps played per game and Pro Football Focus (PFF) score per game were collected for each athlete, which
                                                served as surrogate measures of endurance and performance, respectively. The results were analyzed with
                                                players grouped by position, and then all players grouped as a whole. Within-group comparisons were
                                                performed via t-tests.


                                                Results
                                                A total of 78 players met the criteria for inclusion in the study. The overall mean PFF score pre-COVID-19
                                                infection was 62.15 (SD: 6.93), while it was 61.73 (SD: 7.42) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of
                                                0.42 after infection (n=78, p=0.33). The mean number of snaps played per game pre-COVID-19 infection was
                                                38.99 (SD: 16.46) while it was 38.10 (SD: 17.05) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of 0.89 after
                                                infection (n=78, p=0.30). When grouped by position, statistically significant differences were seen with
                                                Defensive Backs’ mean snaps played per game decreasing by 18.30 (n=6, p=0.03) and Defensive Linemen’s
                                                mean PFF score decreasing by 3.77 points (n=21, p=0.03).


                                                Conclusion
                                                Based on our findings, COVID-19 infection negatively impacted endurance in Defensive Backs, and
                                                performance in Defensive Linemen. However, there was inconclusive evidence to show whether COVID-19
                                                infection negatively impacted other positions when analyzed separately or all positions when analyzed
                                                together. Further studies with more participants are needed to fully assess the effects of COVID-19 on
                                                performance and endurance in elite athletes.



                                                Categories: Physical Medicine & Rehabilitation, Infectious Disease, Orthopedics
                                                Keywords: physical medicine and rehabilitation (pm&r), sports medicine, performance, endurance, athletes, nfl,
                                                football, covid-19



                                                Introduction
                                                As the world struggled to balance normalcy with safety amidst the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)
                                                pandemic, many professional sports leagues reopened in the United States prior to vaccines against the
                                                disease becoming available. One of the earliest examples, the National Football League (NFL), was able to
                                                complete the 2020-2021 season after implementing rigorous testing and isolation protocols, including the
                                                administration of over 600,000 COVID-19 tests over the six-month season [1].


                                                Through these protocols, the NFL was generally able to mitigate large outbreaks, although individual players
                                                still tested positive for the virus. A recent meta-analysis found that acute symptoms are mild or absent in
                                                ~94% of athletes, but 3.8-17% will go on to develop persistent symptoms that may be detrimental to their
                                                performance [2]. This is in line with anecdotal reports of some NFL players experiencing a longer duration of
                                                symptoms leading to diminished on-field performance. Myles Garrett, a two-time NFL All-Pro Defensive
                                                End for the Cleveland Browns, was outspoken about his post-COVID-19 sequela. He was on the COVID-19


                               How to cite this article
                               Walker C R, Belisario J, Abramoff B (March 06, 2023) The Effect of Probable COVID-19 Infection on the National Football League Players’
                               Performance and Endurance During the 2020 Season. Cureus 15(3): e35821. DOI 10.7759/cureus.35821
                                                  Injury Reserve (COVID-IR) list for 11 days. Following this, he reported that he felt he was operating at 50%
                                                 and that fatigue prevented him from performing at his best for extended periods of time [3]. Similar stories
                                                 from other notable professional athletes have been reported, including Jayson Tatum, a three-time National
                                                 Basketball Association (NBA) All-Star who currently plays for the Boston Celtics, and Yoan Moncada who
                                                 plays second base for the Chicago White Sox of Major League Baseball (MLB) [4,5].


                                                 The objective of this study was to evaluate the performance of NFL players before and after a presumed
                                                 positive test for COVID-19 during the 2020-2021 NFL season.


                                                 Materials And Methods
                                                 Study design
                                                 We adopted a retrospective single-arm cohort study design, using individual player data to compare
                                                 performance and endurance pre-COVID-19 infection to performance and endurance post-COVID-19
                                                 infection. The study was deemed exempt by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board.


                                                 Participants
                                                 During the 2020-2021 season, the NFL created a COVID-IR list. This list included players who tested positive
                                                 or had close-contact exposure to someone with COVID-19. Following a high-risk exposure, a player could
                                                 return to team activities after having two negative tests within 24 hours. Following a positive test, an
                                                 asymptomatic player could return to team activities after 10 days since the initial positive test or if he tested
                                                 negative twice at least 24 hours apart. If the player was symptomatic, he could return to team activities after
                                                 10 days from the time symptoms first appeared and after 24 hours since he last experienced symptoms [6].
                                                 For the purposes of this study, a player was considered to have a COVID-19 infection if they were placed on
                                                 the COVID-19 IR list during the 2020-2021 season and were on the list for 10 days or more. Since vaccines
                                                 for COVID-19 were not available during the study period, all participants were considered unvaccinated.


                                                 To exclude players who were placed on the COVID-19 IR list due to high-risk exposure, we excluded any
                                                 player who was on the COVID-19 IR list for less than 10 days. We also excluded players who played in fewer
                                                 than two games either before testing positive or after they returned, to allow for averaging of their
                                                 performance and endurance across multiple games. We also excluded Special Teams players due to the
                                                 limited data available to determine on-field performance.


                                                 All NFL players listed on the NFL’s COVID-IR list during the 2020-2021 season were screened for inclusion.


                                                 Data collection and analysis
                                                 To assess athletic performance, we compared the mean Pro Football Focus (PFF) score per game pre- and
                                                 post-COVID-19 infection. PFF is a commonly used grading system that evaluates individual players based on
                                                 their overall performance in a game. To calculate a player’s PFF score, a panel of professional analysts
                                                 assigns each player a score from -2 to 2 in 0.5 increments for every play that they are on the field for with 0
                                                 being the average or “expected” score. A senior analyst will review all the grades, finalize them, then convert
                                                 the plus-minus grades to an overall score for the game, ranging from 0 to 100, with 0 being the worst and 100
                                                 being the best. PFF evaluates player performance in a standardized manner across all positions, allowing for
                                                 direct comparison [7]. Overall game scores were collected for every player who met the inclusion criteria.
                                                 These scores were then averaged pre- and post-COVID-19 infection for comparison.


                                                 The publicly available number of “snaps” (plays) that each player participated in was used as a proxy of
                                                 player endurance. The overall number of “snaps” that players participated in per game was collected for
                                                 every player who met the inclusion criteria. The number of snaps played per game was then averaged pre-
                                                 and post-COVID-19 infection for comparison.


                                                 Analysis was done for the whole group and by position. Within-group comparisons were performed using t-
                                                 tests. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.


                                                 Results
                                                 A total of 368 players were placed on the COVID-IR list during the season due to high-risk exposures or a
                                                 positive PCR test; 78 of the 368 players met the criteria for probable COVID-19 infection and were included
                                                 in our analysis. The overall mean PFF score pre-COVID-19 infection was 62.15 (SD: 6.93), while it was 61.73
                                                 (SD: 7.42) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of 0.42 after infection (n=78, p=0.33, range: -20.55
                                                 to 18.18). The mean number of snaps played per game pre-COVID-19 infection was 38.99 (SD: 16.46), while
                                                 it was 38.10 (SD: 17.05) post-COVID-19 infection, showing a decrease of 0.89 after infection (n=78, p=0.30,
                                                 range: -48.83 to 49.68).


                                                 When grouped by position, a statistically significant decrease in the mean PFF score was seen among
                                                 Defensive Linemen (mean decrease: 3.77, n=21, p=0.03). A decrease in mean PFF score was also seen among

                                                 kg/m2. Obesity has been correlated with worse COVID-19 symptoms, which may explain this trend [15].
                                                 Running Backs, who sustain the greatest number of severe impacts (>10 G force) per game, had an increase
                                                 in mean PFF score that approached statical significance [13]. We hypothesize that the time away from sport
                                                 allowed them to better recover from the intense physical demands of their position and thus perform better
                                                 upon returning.


                                                 Limitations
                                                 There are numerous confounding factors that exist within an NFL season that may impact an individual
                                                 player’s PFF score or number of snaps played, none of which were able to be analyzed in our study. A few
                                                 examples of confounding factors are injuries to the players or their teammates, trades between teams
                                                 involving the players or their teammates, different game strategies used on a weekly basis, changes in the
                                                 difficulty of the opposition on a weekly basis, and differences in refereeing by in-game officials. Our study
                                                 was further limited by the small number of players that met the inclusion criteria for each position and by
                                                 not having access to NFL testing data and official medical history for the players. Hence, COVID-19-positive
                                                 cases were deduced using the NFL isolation protocol and the amount of time players spent on the COVID-IR
                                                 list, which may have resulted in excluding some true positive cases and failing to differentiate asymptomatic
                                                 cases from symptomatic cases. Lastly, it was impossible to distinguish performance changes due to COVID-
                                                 19 infection vs. changes due to the athlete having several days of rest before returning to sport.


                                                 Conclusions
                                                 Based on our findings, probable COVID-19 infection negatively impacted endurance among Defensive
                                                 Backs, and performance among Defensive Linemen. However, the evidence was inconclusive as to whether
                                                 COVID-19 infection negatively impacted other positions when analyzed separately or all positions when
                                                 analyzed together. Further studies with more participants are warranted to gain deeper insights into the
                                                 effects of COVID-19 on performance and endurance among professional American football athletes.

 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Rehabilitation","Performance"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Adult / Recreational"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Crossover laboratory study of 13 recreationally active male volunteers who performed 5-second isometric Nordic hamstring contractions on a platform inclined at 30 degrees, with knee angles of 30, 50 and 60 degrees and hip angles of 0, 30 and 45 degrees, while surface EMG was recorded. At a hip angle of 0 degrees, biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus activity was higher at a knee angle of 30 degrees than at 50 or 60 degrees (p < 0.05). Semimembranosus activity at knee 60 and hip 45 was higher than at knee 60 and hip 0 (p < 0.05).",
 "screeningLimitations":"The sample was 13 recreationally active men rather than athletes, the contractions were isometric, and the board was inclined at only one angle (30 degrees). The study measures muscle activation only, so it cannot show effects on strength, hamstring injury or return to sport.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the higher EMG at a 30-degree knee angle as proof that this position builds more hamstring strength or prevents injury, when the study measured only isometric muscle activation in recreational men.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Keerasomboon T, Soga T, Hirose N. The Effect of Variations in Knee and Hip Angles on Electromyographic Activity of the Hamstrings and Related Muscles During the Nordic Hamstring Exercise. Int J Sports Phys Ther. 2024;19(3):275-283.",
   "doi":"10.26603/001c.92745",
   "abstract":"The Nordic hamstring exercise is often performed on an inclined board, but isometric hamstring activation across different knee and hip angles has not been well described. The authors measured surface EMG of the hamstrings and related muscles during 5-second isometric Nordic contractions in 13 male volunteers, with knee angles of 30, 50 and 60 degrees and hip angles of 0, 30 and 45 degrees, on a platform inclined at 30 degrees. A knee angle of 30 degrees with hip 0 produced higher activity in three hamstring muscles than knee 50 or 60 degrees.",
   "tldr":"In 13 recreationally active men, isometric Nordic holds with the knee at 30 degrees and the hip at 0 degrees gave higher EMG in three hamstring muscles than knee angles of 50 or 60 degrees. This is an activation result, not a strength or injury result.",
   "methods":"Crossover study. Thirteen male volunteers performed isometric Nordic hamstring contractions on a 30-degree inclined platform at three knee angles (30, 50, 60 degrees) and three hip angles (0, 30, 45 degrees). Knee and hip angles were monitored with an electrical goniometer, and normalised EMG was compared with repeated-measures MANOVA and pairwise tests.",
   "findings":"At a hip angle of 0 degrees, biceps femoris, semitendinosus and semimembranosus EMG was significantly higher at a knee angle of 30 degrees than at 50 or 60 degrees (p < 0.05). Semimembranosus EMG at knee 60 and hip 45 was higher than at knee 60 and hip 0 (p < 0.05). The authors conclude that knee flexion of 30 degrees with hip flexion of 0 degrees was the position giving higher hamstring activation in this set-up.",
   "limitations":"The study had 13 participants, and the authors note the sample was small. The board was inclined only at 30 degrees, which limits generalisation to other board angles or to dynamic Nordic exercise. The study measured isometric EMG only and did not test strength or injury outcomes.",
   "practicalImplications":"When coaches use isometric Nordic holds, a 30-degree knee angle with the hip at 0 degrees produced more hamstring EMG than 50 or 60 degrees in this group of recreational men. Trial the angle with your own athletes before changing programmes, and do not treat EMG as a direct strength or injury measure.",
   "athleteDev":"For strength staff, the study supports treating knee angle as a variable in isometric Nordic work, with 30 degrees and hip 0 giving higher hamstring activation in this sample. Whether this builds strength or reduces injury risk has not been tested.",
   "rtp":"Not directly applicable to return to sport. The participants were uninjured recreational men and the study measured activation only, so it cannot set loads or angles for a rehabilitation or return-to-play plan."
 }
}

Semimembranosus EMG at knee 60 and hip 45 was higher than at knee 60 and hip 0 (p < 0.05). The authors conclude that knee flexion of 30 degrees with hip flexion of 0 degrees was the position giving higher hamstring activation in this set-up.",

The board was inclined only at 30 degrees, which limits generalisation to other board angles or to dynamic Nordic exercise. The study measured isometric EMG only and did not test strength or injury outcomes.",

29	                   The benefit of performing the Nordic Hamstring Exercise (NHE) on an inclined board has
30	                   been described, however, isometric hamstring activation in different knee and hip angles
31	                   has not yet been thoroughly explored.
32	
33	                   Purpose
34	                   This study investigated the effect of variations in knee and hip angles during the
35	                   isometric performance of the NHE on electromyographic activity of the hamstring
36	                   muscles.
37	
38	                   Study design
39	                   Crossover study
40	
41	                   Methods
42	                   Thirteen male volunteers performed isometric contractions during the NHE with the knee
43	                   (30°, 50°, 60°) and the hip (0°, 30°, and 45°) in various angles of flexion on a leg support
44	                   platform which was inclined at 30°. An electrical goniometer was used to monitor the
45	                   knee and hip joint angles during 5-s isometric contractions. A multivariate analysis of
46	                   variance with repeated measures was used to compare normalized electromyographic
47	                   values of each muscle across different knee and hip angles, followed by pairwise
48	                   comparisons.
49	
50	                   Results
51	                   The electromyographic activity of the biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and
52	                   semimembranosus at a knee angle of 30° and hip angle of 0° were significantly higher
53	                   than those observed with a knee angle of 50° and hip angle of 0°, or a knee angle of 60°
54	                   and hip angle of 0° (p<0.05). The electromyographic activity of the semimembranosus at
55	                   a knee angle of 60° and hip angle of 45° was significantly higher than values obtained
56	                   with knee and hip angles of 60° and 0°, respectively (p<0.05).
57	
58	                   Conclusions
59	                   The results indicate that using a knee flexion of 30° and a hip flexion of 0°, while
60	                   isometrically performing the NHE on a platform inclined at 30°, may optimize
61	                   electromyographic activity of the hamstrings.

                   Conclusions
                   The results indicate that using a knee flexion of 30° and a hip flexion of 0°, while
                   isometrically performing the NHE on a platform inclined at 30°, may optimize

 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised, counterbalanced crossover trial in 10 male amateur soccer players completing 60 minutes of a soccer-specific protocol with a 15-minute half-time break. The control was a passive break, and the re-warm-up condition was a passive 12-minute break followed by a 3-minute re-warm-up. The re-warm-up was followed by better 20 m sprint time (3.32 vs 3.42 s, d = 0.6), squat jump height (30.17 vs 26.96 cm, d = 0.6) and countermovement jump height (31.53 vs 28.15 cm, d = 0.7) early in the second half, while perceived exertion was about 2 units higher.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Ten amateur players completed a single soccer-specific protocol rather than match play, so the findings are short-term and small-sample. The effects were acute, and the study did not examine the physiological mechanisms behind them.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the acute sprint and jump gains as a proven match-day advantage, when the trial measured short-term effects in ten amateur players in a simulated protocol.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Fashioni E, Langley B, Page RM. The effectiveness of a practical half-time re-warm-up strategy on performance and the physical response to soccer-specific activity. J Sports Sci. 2020;38(2):140-149.",
   "doi":"10.1080/02640414.2019.1686941",
   "abstract":"The authors compared a half-time re-warm-up with a passive half-time break in 10 male soccer players completing a 60-minute soccer-specific protocol. The re-warm-up improved 20 m sprint time, squat jump and countermovement jump after the re-warm-up and early in the second half, with no significant change in 5 m or 10 m sprint, muscle soreness or PlayerLoad. Ratings of perceived exertion were higher after the re-warm-up.",
   "tldr":"A 3-minute re-warm-up during a 15-minute half-time break improved 20 m sprint and jump performance early in the second half in amateur players. It also raised perceived exertion, and the effects were short-term.",
   "methods":"Randomised, counterbalanced crossover trial with 10 male amateur soccer players. Each completed 4 x 15-minute periods of a soccer-specific protocol with a 15-minute half-time, either passive (control) or passive 12 minutes plus a 3-minute re-warm-up. Sprint, squat jump, countermovement jump, perceived exertion, muscle soreness and PlayerLoad were measured.",
   "findings":"After the re-warm-up and early in the second half, 20 m sprint time was faster (3.32 vs 3.42 s; d = 0.6), squat jump height was greater (30.17 vs 26.96 cm; d = 0.6) and countermovement jump height was greater (31.53 vs 28.15 cm; d = 0.7). Perceived exertion was about 2 units higher after the re-warm-up. No significant changes were found for 5 m or 10 m sprint, muscle soreness or PlayerLoad.",
   "limitations":"Only 10 amateur male players were studied, and the protocol simulated soccer activity rather than match play. The authors identify a limit on transferring the results to matches and say the mechanisms behind the responses were not considered.",
   "practicalImplications":"A short active re-warm-up during half time may restore some sprint and jump performance in the early second half without raising soreness or PlayerLoad. Coaches should weigh this against the higher perceived exertion it adds, and trial the routine with their own squad before adopting it.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports trialling a short active re-warm-up at half time, expecting small acute gains in 20 m sprint and jump performance in the first minutes of the second half. Confirm the effect in your own players before making it routine.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy amateur players and the outcomes were acute performance measures only."
 }
}

The eﬀectiveness of a practical half-time re-warm-up strategy on performance and
the physical response to soccer-speciﬁc activity
Eduardo Fashioni, Ben Langley                       and Richard Michael Page
Sports Injuries Research Group, Dept. of Sport & Physical Activity, Edge Hill University, Ormskirk, Lancashire, UK


    ABSTRACT                                                                                                                          ARTICLE HISTORY
    The aim of this study was to assess the inﬂuence of a half-time (HT) re-warm up (RWU) strategy on                                 Accepted 24 October 2019
    measures of performance and the physical and perceptual response to soccer-speciﬁc activity. Ten male
                                                                                                                                      KEYWORDS
    soccer players completed a control (CON) and RWU trial, in which participants completed 60 min (4 x 15-                           Jump Performance;
    min periods with a 15-min HT interspersing the third and fourth periods) of a soccer-speciﬁc exercise                             Intermittent Activity; Sprint
    protocol. The CON trial comprised a passive 15-min HT, whilst the RWU trial comprised a passive 12-min                            Performance; Active
    period, followed by a 3-min RWU. The RWU elicited an improvement in 20 m sprint times (d= 0.6; CON:                               Recovery
    3.42 ± 0.20 s; RWU: 3.32 ± 0.12 s), and both squat (d= 0.6; CON: 26.96 ± 5.00 cm; RWU: 30.17 ± 5.13 cm) and
    countermovement jump height (d= 0.7; CON: 28.15 ± 4.72 cm; RWU: 31.53 ± 5.43 cm) following the RWU
    and during the initial stages of the second half. No signiﬁcant changes were identiﬁed for 5 m or
    10 m sprint performance, perceived muscle soreness, or PlayerLoadTM. Ratings of perceived exertion
    were however higher (~2 a.u) following the RWU. These data support the use of a HT RWU intervention to
    elicit acute changes in performance.

{
 "id":"Q71",
 "sourceFile":"The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes - Timing considerations.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in the text, 'The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes: Timing considerations', matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Athlete Wellbeing"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Endurance Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised controlled crossover trial of 22 well-trained male athletes or triathletes, each completing a running session and one night of sleep monitoring under three conditions: whole-body cryostimulation (WBC) straight after training at 19:00, WBC one hour before bed at 22:00, or control, one week apart. WBC after training did not change subjective or objective sleep measures compared with control. It did improve cardiac parasympathetic activity, which was greatest the night after the 22:00 exposure, when core body temperature one hour after bedtime was also lowest.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only men were included, one night was measured per condition, and the sample is small, so the findings may not transfer to women or to longer exposure periods. The sleep result is null, so the positive findings rest on autonomic and temperature measures rather than sleep quality itself.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the autonomic and temperature changes as proof that cryostimulation improves sleep, when the sleep measures themselves did not change after training exposure.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Arc-Chagnaud C, Dugué B, Bouzigon R, Pla R, Bosquet L, Dupuy O. The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes: Timing considerations. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024:1-10.",
   "doi":"10.1002/ejsc.12200",
   "abstract":"The study aimed to test whether whole-body cryostimulation after training improves sleep and recovery, and which timing is best: immediately after training or one hour before bed. Twenty-two well-trained male athletes or triathletes completed three randomised crossover sessions. WBC after training did not change subjective or objective sleep, but it improved cardiac parasympathetic activity, which was most evident after the exposure one hour before bed, where core body temperature was also lowest.",
   "tldr":"In trained male endurance athletes, cryostimulation straight after evening training did not change sleep measures. Exposure one hour before bed gave the clearest overnight autonomic and core temperature changes, but sleep quality itself was unchanged.",
   "methods":"Randomised controlled crossover protocol in 22 well-trained male athletes or triathletes. Each completed a running training session and one night of sleep analysis under WBC at 19:00 (after training), WBC at 22:00 (one hour before bed), or control, with sessions spaced seven days apart. Sleep was measured by actimetry, cerebral activity recordings, heart rate variability, core body temperature and perceptual scales.",
   "findings":"WBC after training did not change subjective or objective sleep parameters compared with control. WBC improved cardiac parasympathetic activity, which was greater overnight after the 22:00 exposure than after the other conditions. Core body temperature one hour after bedtime was lowest in the 22:00 condition. The authors also report a condition effect on slow-wave sleep and a decrease in muscle soreness at the 19:00 time point.",
   "limitations":"Only male participants were included, and the authors note that responses in women may differ and that the menstrual cycle was not considered. Each condition was measured over a single night. The sample was small and well-trained, which limits extrapolation to other populations.",
   "practicalImplications":"Cryostimulation straight after evening training did not change sleep in this group, so it should not be marketed as a sleep aid. Using it about one hour before bed may give better overnight autonomic recovery and a larger core temperature drop than exposure straight after training, and staff can test that timing with their own athletes.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study supports trialling whole-body cryostimulation about one hour before bed, rather than straight after an evening session, as a recovery aid for trained male endurance athletes. Track autonomic and temperature responses, because sleep quality itself did not improve.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy, well-trained athletes, and the study cannot show whether cryostimulation helps recovery after injury or during rehabilitation."
 }
}

 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Endurance Sport"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised controlled crossover trial of 22 well-trained male athletes or triathletes, each completing an evening high-intensity running session and one night of sleep monitoring under three conditions: whole-body cryostimulation (WBC) straight after training (about 19:00), WBC one hour before bed (about 22:00), or control, one week apart. No sleep measure (headband, actigraphy or questionnaire) differed between conditions. Parasympathetic heart rate variability indices were higher only during a 10-minute slow-wave sleep window, mainly after the 22:00 exposure, when core body temperature after bedtime was also lowest.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only men were included, one night was measured per condition, and the sample is small, so the findings may not transfer to women or to longer exposure periods. The sleep result is null, so the positive findings rest on heart rate variability in a short deep-sleep window and on temperature rather than on sleep quality itself.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the autonomic and temperature changes as proof that cryostimulation improves sleep, when no sleep measure changed under either exposure timing.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Arc-Chagnaud C, Dugué B, Bouzigon R, Pla R, Bosquet L, D-day Consortium, et al. The effectiveness of cryostimulation exposure on sleep and recovery in male athletes: Timing considerations. Eur J Sport Sci. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.1002/ejsc.12200",
   "abstract":"The study aimed to test whether whole-body cryostimulation after training improves sleep and recovery, and which timing is best: immediately after training or one hour before bed. Twenty-two well-trained male athletes or triathletes completed three randomised crossover sessions. WBC did not change subjective or objective sleep, but it increased cardiac parasympathetic activity during deep sleep, most clearly after the exposure one hour before bed, where core body temperature was also lowest.",
   "tldr":"In trained male endurance athletes, cryostimulation after evening training did not change any sleep measure, whether given straight after training or one hour before bed. The before-bed timing gave the clearest deep-sleep heart rate variability and core temperature changes.",
   "methods":"Randomised controlled crossover protocol in 22 well-trained male athletes or triathletes, run in winter with outdoor training at 5 to 10 C. Each completed a 70-minute interval running session at 18:00 and one night of home sleep analysis under WBC after training, WBC one hour before their own bedtime, or control, with sessions seven days apart; WBC was 30 s at -25 C then 3 min at -70 C. Sleep was measured with an EEG headband, wrist actigraphy, overnight heart rate variability, an ingested temperature pill and perceptual scales, analysed with two-way repeated-measures ANOVA.",
   "findings":"No sleep parameter differed between the three nights, including total sleep time, slow-wave sleep, sleep efficiency, movements and perceived sleep quality. Heart rate variability showed a condition effect only in the 10-minute slow-wave sleep window, with RMSSD, PNS index, SD1 and LF/HF favouring the 22:00 condition over control; whole-night and first-4-hour values did not differ. Core body temperature fell more after bedtime in the 22:00 condition, and muscle soreness and perceived recovery did not differ significantly between conditions.",
   "limitations":"Only male participants were included, and the authors note that responses in women may differ and that the menstrual cycle was not considered. Each condition was measured over a single night in good sleepers during winter, which the authors say may not favour detecting sleep effects. The sample was small and well-trained, which limits extrapolation to other populations.",
   "practicalImplications":"Cryostimulation after evening training did not change sleep in this group at either timing, so the data do not support using it as a sleep aid. If it is used for recovery, exposure about one hour before bed produced larger deep-sleep parasympathetic and core temperature changes than exposure straight after training.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff using whole-body cryostimulation with trained male endurance athletes, the study suggests a session about one hour before bed gives stronger overnight autonomic and temperature responses than one straight after an evening session. Whether these responses improve next-day performance was not tested.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. The participants were healthy, well-trained athletes, and the study cannot show whether cryostimulation helps recovery after injury or during rehabilitation."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "findings: 'condition effect on slow-wave sleep' was wrong -> the condition effect was in heart rate variability during the slow-wave sleep window ('The ANOVA test revealed a condition effect only in the SWS period'); SWS duration did not differ ('We found no difference for any outcome variable between the three nights')",
     "findings: 'decrease in muscle soreness at the 19:00 time point' presented as a finding -> soreness change was non-significant ('We found no statistical effect of WBC on muscle soreness or perceived recovery')",
     "evidenceSummary/abstract: parasympathetic effect limited to the SWS window; whole-night and 4 h HRV were 'ns' (Table 2)",
     "citation: removed online-first placeholder pages '1-10'; added D-day Consortium as printed in the author line",
     "practicalImplications/athleteDev: removed generic 'test that timing with your own athletes' and 'track responses' advice; stated that performance effects were not tested"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"The paper's Highlights state 'Cryotherapy improves sleep through better parasympathetic activation', which its own sleep results do not support. Online-first version: no volume or issue printed; year taken from the 'Eur J Sport Sci. 2024' line.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}

 "evidenceSummary":"Parallel-group randomised trial in 18 analysed U-21 Mexican National Team players (20 recruited; goalkeepers and players who missed training camp sessions were excluded). After an unofficial game and the day after, one group used a carbohydrate-protein shake, foam roller, cold-water immersion and tart cherry juice, and the other used the shake, stretching and intermittent cold-water immersion. Creatine kinase was back to normal by 68 h post-game and neuromuscular and perceptual measures had levelled out by 44 h, with no statistically significant difference between the two protocols.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only male players were studied, the sample is small, and there was no control group, so the trial cannot show whether either protocol beats no intervention. The abstract and methods also disagree on the sample (18 players aged 19.56 years in the abstract; 20 recruited players aged 20 years in the methods).",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the within-group changes seen only with the foam roller and tart cherry protocol as proof that it recovers players better, when the between-protocol comparison was not significant.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Altarriba-Bartes A, Vicens-Bordas J, Peña J, Alarcón-Palacios F, Sixtos-Meliton LA, Matabosch-Pijuan M, et al. The effectiveness of two comprehensive recovery protocols on performance and physiological measures in elite soccer players: A parallel group-randomized trial. Int J Sports Sci Coach. 2023:1-11.",
   "doi":"10.1177/17479541231155585",
   "abstract":"The authors compared two comprehensive post-game recovery protocols in 18 players from the Mexican U-21 national team, randomised to a foam roller and tart cherry protocol or a stretching protocol, both with a carbohydrate-protein shake and intermittent cold-water immersion. Creatine kinase, jump, hamstring strength, perceived recovery and soreness were measured up to 68 h after a game. Both protocols showed time effects, and no significant differences were found between them.",
   "tldr":"Two broad post-game recovery combinations were similarly effective in elite young players for creatine kinase, neuromuscular and soreness measures. Neither was shown to beat no intervention, because the trial had no control group.",
   "methods":"Parallel-group randomised trial with block randomisation, with players matched by position. Players were allocated to protocol (a), a carbohydrate-protein shake, foam roller, cold-water immersion and tart cherry juice concentrate (n = 9), or protocol (b), a shake, stretching and intermittent cold-water immersion (n = 9), after an unofficial game and the day after. Creatine kinase, countermovement jump, hamstring maximal voluntary contraction, perceived recovery and soreness were measured before, immediately after, and at 20, 44 and 68 h post-game.",
   "findings":"Both protocols showed significant time effects. Creatine kinase normalised entirely by 68 h post-game, and neuromuscular and perceptual outcomes levelled out by 44 h. No significant between-protocol effects were found. Only protocol (a) showed interaction changes, in neuromuscular function and muscle soreness at post-game and 20 h. Creatine kinase correlated strongly with accelerations, decelerations, sprints and high-speed running distance.",
   "limitations":"Only male players were studied, the sample was small, and there was no control group, so the trial cannot show whether either protocol is more effective than no intervention. The abstract (18 players, 19.56 years) and methods (20 players recruited, 20 years, with goalkeepers and players who missed camp sessions excluded) describe the sample differently. The authors note that enrolling professional players is a common limitation of this design.",
   "practicalImplications":"After a game, both recovery combinations in this trial produced similar changes in creatine kinase, neuromuscular function and soreness. Staff can choose the combination that fits their players and facilities, and should use creatine kinase trends alongside match running and sprint loads when judging recovery.",
   "athleteDev":"For performance staff, the study suggests either recovery combination can be used after games for elite young male players, and creatine kinase tracks running and sprint loads closely enough to be used alongside GPS data when judging recovery.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. The players were uninjured national-team members, and the study measured post-game recovery markers only, so it cannot guide rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions."
 }
}

Abstract
Elite soccer players consistently report using several recovery methods after practices and games. However, it is unclear how
their subsequent performance could be enhanced using broad protocols. The aim of this study was to compare the effectiveness
of two different comprehensive recovery protocols in physiological, neuromuscular, and perceptual outcomes. Eighteen Mexican
National Team players (19.56 ± 0.62 years) were recruited. Using a randomized parallel group design, players followed one of
two recovery protocols: (a) carbohydrate and protein shake, foam roller, cold-water immersion, and tart cherry juice concen-
trate (n = 9) or (b) carbohydrate and protein shake, stretching, and intermittent cold-water immersion (n = 9) following the
completion of an unofﬁcial game and the day after. Muscular creatine kinase, countermovement jump, hamstring maximal vol-
untary contraction, perceived recovery, and muscle soreness were assessed before, immediately after, and 20-44-68 h post-
game. Signiﬁcant effects (set at ρ≤0.05) of time were present in both interventions. Muscular creatine kinase was normalized
entirely at 68 h post-game, while neuromuscular and perceptual outcomes were homogenized at 44 h. No statistically signiﬁcant
effects between protocols were found. Still, the interaction effects showed changes only in the group using protocol (a) at post-
game and 20 h after in neuromuscular and muscle soreness. There were large correlations between muscular creatine kinase
and accelerations, decelerations, sprints, and high-speed running distances. In conclusion, the interventions are equally effective
for improving physiological, neuromuscular, and perceptual outcomes. Thus, elite soccer players may beneﬁt from different com-
binations of methods after practices or games to obtain positive effects on recovery after them.

Association football, carbohydrate and protein shake, cherry juice, cold-water immersion, creatine kinase, foam roller,

 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review of electronic databases (Medline Complete, SPORTDiscus, Embase; final search 11 October 2022) of 38 studies from 37 records, with 403 participants of whom 361 were male. Of these, 22 studies assessed exercise performance or capacity, with time-trial improvements in 2 studies (5.7-11.4%) and increased exercise capacity in 5 (14.3-26.2%). During constant work rate exercise, 9 studies reported lower heart rate and 8 reported lower core temperature, and 10 reported higher plasma volume; gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 26 studies.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The evidence is mostly from males (about 90% of participants), with only one female-only study, few endurance running studies and few field studies.    "year":2023,
   "citation":"Jardine WT, Aisbett B, Kelly MK, Burke LM, Ross ML, Condo D, et al. The Effect of Pre-Exercise Hyperhydration on Exercise Performance, Physiological Outcomes and Gastrointestinal Symptoms: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2023.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-023-01885-2",
   "abstract":"Pre-exercise hyperhydration with osmotic aids is proposed to offset dehydration and heat stress during prolonged exercise in the heat. The authors searched three databases for English full-text studies comparing hyperhydration with a baseline or placebo condition, and rated study quality with the American Dietetic Association checklist. Thirty-eight studies were included. Hyperhydration may improve capacity during constant work rate exercise, which the authors attribute to lower heart rate and core temperature alongside higher plasma volume, and gastrointestinal symptoms varied across studies.",
   "tldr":"Pre-exercise hyperhydration may help capacity in constant-pace exercise in the heat, possibly by lowering heart rate and core temperature. The evidence is mostly from male participants, and gut symptoms vary widely.",
   "methods":"Systematic review of Medline Complete, SPORTDiscus and Embase (final search 11 October 2022) for English full-text studies comparing a hyperhydration intervention with baseline or placebo. Exercise studies had to involve at least recreational athletes (training at least three times and 5 h per week). Study quality was assessed with the American Dietetic Association Quality Criteria Checklist, with two authors screening and rating quality.",
   "findings":"Of 38 studies (403 participants, 361 male), 22 assessed performance or capacity. Two studies reported time-trial improvements (5.7-11.4%), three reported more work completed (4-5%), and five of seven time-to-exhaustion studies reported higher exercise capacity (14.3-26.2%). Nine studies reported lower mean heart rate during constant work rate exercise, eight reported lower mean core temperature, and ten reported higher plasma volume. Gastrointestinal symptoms were reported in 26 studies.",
   "limitations":"Most participants were male, and only one study included females only, with none adequately accounting for menstrual cycle phase. Few studies examined endurance running or field settings, and the capacity gains come from time-to-exhaustion tests, which the authors note are less reliable than time-trials. Gastrointestinal symptoms were not assessed with validated, reliable tools.",
   "practicalImplications":"In hot conditions, a hyperhydration protocol may help steady-pace endurance work, with lower heart rate and core temperature reported in several studies, but performance gains are reported in only a few studies. The review notes that splitting the dose into smaller aliquots did not increase gut symptoms, and symptoms may vary with product, dose and ingestion rate.",
   "athleteDev":"For endurance performance staff, the review supports testing pre-exercise hyperhydration as a heat strategy for constant-pace efforts, with attention to fluid retention and gut comfort. Expect the clearest effects on heart rate and core temperature rather than guaranteed time-trial gains.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable to return to sport. The review covers healthy athletes in performance trials in the heat and does not address injury, rehabilitation or clearance decisions."
